analysis.one_liner: Bans banks from trading for their own profit with government-backed deposits.
analysis.headline: The Senate Banking Committee never brought the bill to a vote, but the same ban on bank trading became law a few months later inside the broader financial overhaul known as the Volcker Rule.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would forbid banks that hold insured deposits from "proprietary trading" — using the bank's own money to bet on stocks, bonds, derivatives, and other securities for its own profit. It would also bar banks from owning, sponsoring, or serving as investment manager for hedge funds and private equity funds, and it would stop underwriters of mortgage-backed and other asset-backed securities from making trades that conflict with the investors who bought those securities. The aim is to separate the government-backstopped, deposit-taking side of banking from the high-risk trading side, so that another trading collapse cannot again threaten bank deposits and taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors, bank customers, and taxpayers stand to benefit, because the bill removes government-insured deposits and federal backstops from high-risk trading. Investors in asset-backed securities also benefit, since the bill bans the underwriters of those securities from trading in ways that conflict with the investors who bought them — the practice at the heart of the 2008 crisis, where banks sold bonds tied to mortgages while positioning against them.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any banking entity — insured banks and the companies that control them — from engaging in proprietary trading, meaning betting the bank's own capital on securities, derivatives, and swaps.

Bars banking entities from taking or retaining any ownership interest in, or sponsoring, a hedge fund or private equity fund, and forbids a bank that manages such a fund from providing it prime brokerage or other services — ending the tangle of hidden bank exposures to unregistered funds.

Subjects any Federal Reserve-supervised nonbank financial company that engages in this trading to extra capital requirements and quantitative limits, so the ban cannot be dodged simply by keeping the trading outside a bank charter.

Prohibits an underwriter, placement agent, or sponsor of an asset-backed security from any transaction that creates a material conflict of interest with investors or undermines the security's value — directly targeting banks that sell bonds to investors and simultaneously bet against them.

Allows regulators to exempt client-serving activities like market-making, underwriting, and hedging, and purchases of Treasury, agency, and municipal obligations — but only where the activity poses no conflict of interest, no high-risk exposure, and no threat to the firm's safety or U.S. financial stability.

analysis.who_pays: Large Wall Street banks bear the main cost: they lose the profits from deposit-backed proprietary trading desks, from owning or sponsoring hedge funds and private equity funds, and from trades that conflict with securities they have sold to investors. Hedge funds and private equity funds lose a channel of bank capital, sponsorship, and services. Some of the lost trading activity may show up as somewhat higher costs for bank clients.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big banks and their trading desks

drawbacks.text: The bill lets regulators exempt client-serving market-making, underwriting, and hedging from the ban, which forces them to draw a line between trading that serves customers and trading for the bank's own account — a line that is genuinely hard to police and invites argument over every trade.

The ban applies to banks and to nonbank financial companies that the Federal Reserve supervises, so trading could migrate to firms outside that perimeter; the bill's extra capital and limits reach only Fed-supervised nonbanks.

Ending bank ownership of, sponsorship of, and prime-brokerage services to hedge funds and private equity funds removes a source of capital and financing for those funds, which raises their cost of operating.

Forfeiting trading and fund income reduces the earnings of the affected banks, which their shareholders absorb directly and which supporters of the banks argued could modestly reduce their capacity to extend credit to customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is structural: it removes a repeat of the arrangement that turned a trading crisis into a taxpayer crisis, by walling off government-insured deposits from the trading desk. The costs are real but narrower — some lost bank profits, a harder compliance job for regulators, and possibly somewhat higher trading costs for clients — and the bill's carve-outs for client service, hedging, and government obligations are designed to preserve normal banking business. On balance the protection for depositors and taxpayers outweighs the costs, which fall mostly on the banks' own shareholders.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a markup or a vote; a few months later Congress passed a larger financial regulation law containing the same proprietary trading ban, which became known as the Volcker Rule.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley of Oregon introduced the bill on March 10, 2010, joined by four other Democratic senators: Carl Levin, Ted Kaufman, Sherrod Brown of Ohio, and Jeanne Shaheen.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs that same day; no further action was ever taken on it.
Seven Senate Democrats had signed on as cosponsors by the end, but the committee never held a markup and the bill never reached the Senate floor.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2011 with the bill still sitting in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For this standalone bill, no one escaped scrutiny: the identical ban was written into the broader Dodd-Frank financial regulation law that became law in mid-2010 as the Volcker Rule, so big banks gained only a few extra months of unrestricted deposit-backed trading rather than a lasting reprieve. Depositors and taxpayers got substantially the same protection through the larger law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big banks, for only a few months

for.name: Sens. Carl Levin, Ted Kaufman, Sherrod Brown, and Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Joined Merkley in introducing the bill in the Senate.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: In January 2010 publicly endorsed banning deposit-insured banks from proprietary trading and pressed for it in the financial regulation bill, which prompted Merkley and Levin to draft this version.

against.name: Chair Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chairman, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred to his committee; no markup was scheduled and the bill died there.

against.name: Wall Street banks and financial industry lobbyists
against.role: Opponents of the proprietary trading ban
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against restricting bank trading and fund ownership and sought to shape the eventual rule's exemptions and definitions.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded, so no roll call exists; the bill's eight sponsors and cosponsors were all Senate Democrats, and the broader law that carried the same ban passed months later along largely party lines.

industries.industry: Large Wall Street banks and their trading operations
industries.note: The bill bans banking entities from proprietary trading and from owning or sponsoring hedge funds and private equity funds, ending revenue earned by putting deposit-insured bank capital at risk. That revenue came alongside a federal safety net on the bank's liabilities, so the industry's interest ran directly against the protection of depositors and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity funds
industries.note: Banks could no longer invest in, sponsor, manage, or serve as prime broker to these funds, cutting off a major channel of bank capital and services and severing the bank-name sponsorship several large funds relied on.

The bill prohibits underwriters, placement agents, and sponsors of asset-backed securities from trading in ways that conflict with investors in, or undermine the value of, the securities they sold — ending a profitable practice of selling mortgage bonds while betting against them.
Unlike banks, these companies may keep proprietary trading and fund stakes, but only under added capital requirements and quantitative limits, so they retain the activity at a higher cost.
